details.exam_pattern: Medium-High. The latest two papers share the same two-section format: answer two of three questions in each section. Section A repeatedly covers clock synchronisation, scheduling and POSIX-style real-time systems; Section B repeatedly covers QUIC, latency, congestion and soft real-time applications. Older papers are still useful for coverage, but the recent pair is the strongest prediction evidence.
details.title: CT420 - Real Time Systems
drill: Prioritise the 2024/25 and 2025/26 format: two sections, choose two of three questions in each. Predict topic families, not an exact question slot.
Time synchronisation is the safest area: NTP, PTP, offset/delay calculations, ntpq output, boundary/transparent clocks, BMCA and logical clocks.
Scheduling is consistently examinable: cyclic executives, overrun detection, Rate Monotonic, EDF, schedulability, WCET and loop/longest-path reasoning.
Concurrency and priority protocols recur: priority inheritance/ceiling, deadlock, semaphores, memory locking and POSIX-style real-time concerns.
Fault tolerance/redundancy is more historical but still worth background revision: RAID, Hamming/SEC, hardware redundancy, voters and Java exception examples.
Recent Section B repeatedly favours soft real-time/web protocol material: QUIC, TCP head-of-line blocking, congestion control, latency, adaptive streaming, Wireshark/qLog/qViz and cloud-gaming cases.
details.paper_format: choose two of three questions in each
details.name: Real Time Systems

families.title: Time Synchronisation, Clocks, NTP And PTP
appearances: 2025/26 – Q1(a) lunar localisation stack [5]; Q1(b) PTP hardware timestamps, transparent clocks and P2P delay [6]; Q1(c) Berkeley algorithm [4].
2024/25 – Q1(a) accuracy, stability, offset and skew [5]; Q1(b) clock handler with skew compensation [5]; Q1(c) Berkeley [5]. Q2(b) PTP mechanisms [5].
2023/24 – Q3(b) PTP master, transparent clock and slave, including correction data and an offset or delay calculation [5].
2022/23 – Q3(a) Berkeley and UTC suitability [5]; Q4(b) PTP hardware timing, transparent clocks and P2P calculation [7].
2021/22 – Q1 PTP architecture, E2E/P2P, boundary and transparent clocks, BMCA redundancy, and NTP backup [20].
families.question: For a distributed system requiring accurate clocks, choose and explain an NTP, PTP, or Berkeley design. Show the relevant messages and timestamps or calculation, then state the assumption or limitation that bounds the claimed accuracy.
families.answer: Reusable answer frame: Define the timing need and required accuracy. For NTP, label t 1 to t 4 , calculate RTD = ( t 4 − t 1 ) − ( t 3 − t 2 ) and state the offset convention. For PTP, draw grandmaster → boundary or transparent clock → slave; explain hardware timestamping, Sync/Follow_Up, delay messages, residence-time correction, and BMCA where relevant. State that asymmetric paths, software delay, bad clock selection, or a missing external reference can bias the result. Berkeley averages internal clocks; it does not by itself supply UTC.

families.title: Cyclic Executives, RM, EDF And Schedulability
appearances: 2025/26 – Q2(c) RM analysis and schedule over [0, 400] [5]; Q3(a) cyclic-executive pseudo-code that detects and counts overruns [5].
2024/25 – Q2(c) RM analysis and schedule [5]; Q3(a) cyclic executive with overrun detection [5].
2023/24 – compulsory Q1: construct CE, RM and EDF schedules, compare them, then implement the CE and detect asynchronous-interrupt overruns [20].
2022/23 – Q1(c) construct an EDF-feasible but not RM-feasible four-task set, validate with utilisation, timeline and RM analysis [7]; Q3(c) CE and interrupt mitigation [6].
2021/22 – CE code and timeline, available interrupt time, plus WCET / longest-path reasoning.
families.question: Given periodic tasks, construct or analyse the stated CE, RM, or EDF schedule. Show the timeline and all arithmetic, then explain what a pass or failure proves under the stated assumptions.
families.answer: Reusable answer frame: Tabulate each task’s execution time C , period T , deadline D , and priority. Calculate U = Σ( C i / T i ). For RM, order by shortest period and use the requested bound or response-time recurrence; a failed sufficient bound is inconclusive, not automatic failure. For EDF with D = T on one ideal processor, use U ≤ 1. Draw the requested interval or hyperperiod. For CE pseudo-code, show the frame loop, task calls, elapsed-time check, and an overrun counter or recovery action. State assumptions about pre-emption, blocking, overhead, releases, and deadlines.

families.title: POSIX Real-Time Support, Concurrency And Priority Protocols
appearances: 2025/26 – Q2(a) select four POSIX-style RTOS capabilities [6]; Q3(b) control a critical region with a mutex / binary semaphore [5]; Q3(c) memory locking and the seven-state model [5].
2024/25 – Q3(b) benefits of Priority Inheritance with a diagram [5]; Q3(c) memory locking and consequences of not using it [5].
2023/24 – Q3(a) CE overrun detection and Q3(b) Priority Inheritance [5 each].
2022/23 and 2021/22 – Priority Ceiling preventing deadlock with shared resources; POSIX.4 signals and sigqueue .
families.question: Explain a real-time resource-management failure using a timeline or process model, then show the POSIX mechanism or priority protocol that bounds, prevents, or exposes it.
families.answer: Reusable answer frame: Identify the high-, medium-, and low-priority tasks and the shared resource. Draw the causal timeline. For priority inversion, explain how a medium task delays the low-priority lock holder while the high-priority task waits; Priority Inheritance temporarily boosts the holder. For a Priority Ceiling answer, show how the unsafe second acquisition is blocked before circular wait. For memory locking, connect paging to a state transition and unbounded delay; explain mlock / mlockall in pseudo-code and the risk of locking too much memory. Include a trade-off: bounded blocking is not no blocking, and protocols do not remove the need for short critical sections.

families.title: QUIC, HTTP/2, HTTP/3, Congestion And Protocol Analysis
appearances: 2025/26 – Q4 TCP head-of-line blocking and QUIC [7], ABR streaming [8]; Q5 qLog/qViz [4], congestion-control fairness [5], QUIC encryption [6]; Q6 cloud gaming, connection migration, congestion control and loss recovery [15].
2024/25 – Q4 HTTP/1 → HTTP/2 and three HTTP/2 features [7], QUIC-versus-TCP establishment and latency [8]; Q5 Wireshark, qLog, qViz and QUIC congestion control [15].
2023/24 – compulsory Q4 QUIC establishment, multiplexing / TCP head-of-line blocking, and congestion control [20]; Q5 Wireshark limitations, qLog/qViz, and resource waterfalls [10].
families.question: Connect a QUIC or HTTP design feature to a concrete latency, loss, multiplexing, monitoring, or congestion symptom in a soft real-time system. State both the improvement and what it does not solve.
families.answer: Reusable answer frame: Name the stack correctly: HTTP/2 multiplexes over one ordered TCP byte stream; HTTP/3 uses QUIC over UDP. Explain that TCP loss can create transport-level head-of-line blocking for unrelated HTTP/2 streams, whereas QUIC independently orders streams. Draw the connection-establishment round trips if asked. Then cover the relevant mechanism: encrypted transport metadata, congestion control, loss recovery, connection migration, qLog endpoint events, qViz visualisation, or Wireshark’s limits with encrypted traffic. Finish with the limitation: QUIC does not eliminate packet loss, RTT, server work, shared congestion, or monitoring requirements.

families.title: Soft Real-Time, QoS, Streaming And Cloud Gaming
appearances: 2025/26 – Q4(b) adaptive-bitrate streaming, estimation, quality–latency trade-offs, and why ABR is insufficient for interactive use [8]; Q6 cloud-gaming end-to-end delay [5].
2024/25 – Q4(b) latency in soft real-time systems [8]; Q6 QoS versus perceived / intrinsic QoS, jitter buffers, and cloud-gaming response delay [15].
2023/24 – compulsory Q4 asks about latency in soft real-time systems [7].
families.question: For an interactive media or cloud-gaming case, decompose end-to-end delay, distinguish measurable delivery quality from user experience, then propose controls and their trade-offs.
families.answer: Reusable answer frame: Decompose delay into input / capture, encoding or processing, queueing, network transmission, loss recovery, decoding, buffering, and playout. Distinguish latency, jitter, loss, throughput, intrinsic QoS, and perceived QoS / QoE. Select a control matched to the symptom: adaptive bitrate, jitter buffer, priority queueing, congestion control, or a shorter encode / playout path. Explain the trade-off: a larger buffer smooths jitter but increases interaction delay; higher quality consumes more bandwidth; retransmission may arrive too late for real-time media.

families.title: Error Detection, Redundancy And Recovery
appearances: 2025/26 – Q2(b) Hamming Distance for Hamming (7, 4) and 8-bit ASCII with parity [4].
2023/24 and 2021/22 – Hamming (7, 4) error detection and correction.
2022/23 – RAID-0/1/5 [4] and backward recovery in dynamic software redundancy [3].
families.question: Choose or explain an error-control or redundancy mechanism, identify which fault or error it covers, and state the independence or coverage assumption it needs.
families.answer: Reusable answer frame: Define fault → error → failure. For Hamming questions, state the codeword length, number of data / parity bits, and the minimum Hamming distance; show which detection or correction claim follows from it. For RAID, distinguish striping, mirroring, and distributed parity as well as performance and failure trade-offs. For voters and replicas, specify the voter rule and explain common-mode failure: replicas are not independent merely because there are several of them. For backward recovery, show the saved consistent state, failure detection, rollback, and the problem of already-emitted external effects.

cards.front: Define clock accuracy, stability, offset, and skew.
cards.back: Accuracy is closeness to a reference clock; stability is consistency of an oscillator’s rate over time and conditions; offset is the instantaneous difference between clocks; skew is the rate at which that offset changes.

cards.front: How does a quartz-based computer clock develop offset and skew?
cards.back: A quartz oscillator drives periodic timer ticks. A frequency error accumulates into clock offset; a roughly constant frequency error is skew. Temperature, ageing, and jitter change the rate, while isolated outliers usually indicate a separate disturbance or correction.

cards.front: What must a skew-compensating clock handler do?
cards.back: On each bounded timer interrupt, add the nominal tick plus a signed correction to the stored time, normalise nanoseconds into seconds, and update the correction from a synchronisation estimate. State the sign convention and avoid unbounded work in the handler.

cards.front: How does the Berkeley algorithm synchronise clocks?
cards.back: A coordinator polls clocks, discards unusable outliers, averages the remaining offsets, then sends each clock a correction. It synchronises a group internally; it needs an external reference if the group must track UTC.

cards.front: When should NTP and PTP work together, and why is NTP robust?
cards.back: NTP filters and selects among multiple hierarchical sources, making it robust and widely deployable for millisecond-scale time or backup reference. Use PTP, with suitable hardware and network support, where tighter synchronisation is required. Explain the accuracy target, redundancy, and failure mode.

cards.front: What should an ntpq comparison discuss?
cards.back: Discuss the selected peer ( * ), reachability, redundancy, stratum, delay, offset, and jitter. reach is an octal history of successful polls. Choose using the whole picture, not one column.

cards.front: What is a sound PTP architecture answer?
cards.back: Identify the grandmaster, ordinary clocks, any boundary or transparent clocks, and the timing domain. The BMCA elects the best master and supports failover; separate domains isolate different timing uses on the same network.

cards.front: How do two-step PTP messages yield delay and offset?
cards.back: Master sends Sync at t 1 ; slave receives at t 2 ; Follow_Up supplies exact t 1 . Slave sends Delay_Req at t 3 ; master receives at t 4 . Assuming symmetric delay, d = (( t 2 − t 1 ) + ( t 4 − t 3 )) / 2 and slave offset = ( t 2 − t 1 ) − d .

cards.front: Why do hardware timestamps, boundary clocks, and transparent clocks improve PTP?
cards.back: Hardware timestamps close to the NIC reduce variable software delay. A boundary clock synchronises upstream and serves downstream. A transparent switch adds its residence time to the correction field; it is not a grandmaster.

cards.front: P2P versus E2E delay measurement in PTP?
cards.back: E2E uses Delay_Req and Delay_Resp to estimate the complete master–slave path. P2P uses Pdelay messages to measure each adjacent link, with suitable switch support and asymmetry treatment.

cards.front: How do lunar GNSS and hyperbolic radio navigation find position?
cards.back: Both turn signal travel time into distance or range difference. GNSS uses multilateration from several timed satellite signals; hyperbolic radio navigation uses time-difference-of-arrival from a master and slaves. Discuss clock synchronisation, geometry, and whether a local differential reference is available.

cards.front: Perfect network versus deterministic network?
cards.back: A perfect network is an idealisation with flawless delivery. A deterministic network provides stated, bounded behaviour such as delay and jitter. Ordinary Ethernet needs controlled traffic to offer useful bounds; contention and radio conditions make Wi-Fi much less predictable.

cards.front: What do C , T , and D represent for a periodic task?
cards.back: C is execution time, using WCET for a proof; T is the period or minimum inter-arrival time; D is the relative deadline. State when an assumption such as D = T is used.

cards.front: What are utilisation and the hyperperiod?
cards.back: U = Σ( C i / T i ). The hyperperiod is LCM( T 1 , T 2 , …), after which periodic releases repeat. Both are starting points, not a substitute for the requested analysis.

cards.front: What is a cyclic executive?
cards.back: A static, table-driven schedule of task calls in fixed frames. It is highly predictable, but less flexible when releases, execution times, or asynchronous events change.

cards.front: How should cyclic-executive code detect and count overruns?
cards.back: Record a frame or cycle start time, run the planned tasks, compare elapsed time with the frame budget, then increment an overrun counter and perform the specified recovery or reporting action when late. Keep the timing check explicit.

cards.front: How does Rate Monotonic assign priority?
cards.back: RM gives the shortest-period task the highest fixed priority. It is analysed for periodic, independent, pre-emptible tasks under stated deadline, overhead, and blocking assumptions.

cards.front: How do you perform the RM response-time analysis for W 4 ?
cards.back: Start with W 4 (0) = C 4 . Iterate W 4 (k+1) = C 4 + Σ j∈hp(4) ⌈ W 4 (k) / T j ⌉ C j until it stabilises or exceeds D 4 . Show every checkpoint.

cards.front: What does the RM utilisation bound prove?
cards.back: For n periodic tasks with D = T , U ≤ n (2 1/ n − 1) is sufficient for RM schedulability. Failing the bound is inconclusive; then use response-time analysis or the requested schedule.

cards.front: How does EDF schedule, and when is it feasible?
cards.back: Earliest Deadline First gives the ready job with the earliest absolute deadline the highest dynamic priority. On one ideal pre-emptive processor with independent periodic tasks, D = T , and negligible overhead, EDF is feasible when U ≤ 1.

cards.front: How can a task set be EDF schedulable but not RM schedulable?
cards.back: Use unequal relative deadlines so the RM fixed-priority ordering creates a missed deadline while EDF can order jobs by their actual absolute deadlines. Validate the set with utilisation, a timeline, and the RM analysis—do not merely assert it.

cards.front: What must a scheduling answer show for marks?
cards.back: List task data and assumptions; show the arithmetic; draw a labelled timeline over the requested interval; identify misses or the fixed point; and state the conclusion. A correct policy name alone is not an analysis.

cards.front: How do you estimate WCET from code?
cards.back: Bound every loop and recursion, identify feasible branches, sum the longest feasible path, and include relevant interrupt, cache, I/O, or blocking effects. Average execution time is not WCET.

cards.front: Name four RTOS or POSIX-style capabilities worth justifying.
cards.back: Choose four relevant capabilities: deterministic priority scheduling, high-resolution clocks and timers, IPC or signals, memory locking, synchronisation primitives, predictable I/O, and bounded interrupt handling. Tie each one to a real-time requirement.

cards.front: What is the safe mutex pattern for a critical region?
cards.back: Initialise the mutex; lock(m) ; access the shared state in a short critical region; unlock(m) on every path. State what blocks, who owns the lock, and avoid holding it across slow or unbounded work.

cards.front: What is priority inversion?
cards.back: A high-priority task waits for a lock held by a low-priority task while medium-priority work can pre-empt the lock holder, extending the high-priority task’s delay.

cards.front: How does Priority Inheritance solve priority inversion?
cards.back: The low-priority lock holder temporarily inherits the blocked high-priority task’s priority, so medium-priority tasks cannot extend the inversion until the lock is released. Draw holder, blocked task, interferer, lock and unlock points.

cards.front: How does the Priority Ceiling Protocol prevent deadlock?
cards.back: Each resource has a ceiling based on its potential users. The protocol blocks an unsafe acquisition before circular wait can form, bounding blocking and preventing deadlock. Show the resources, ceilings, attempted second acquisition, and resulting block.

cards.front: Why use memory locking in a hard real-time process?
cards.back: Locking the verified real-time working set into RAM prevents a page fault causing an unbounded delay on the critical path. Connect the call such as mlockall to the seven-state process model and the avoided blocked state.

cards.front: Why is locking memory too generously a problem?
cards.back: It removes pages from general reclamation, raises pressure on the rest of the system, and may require privilege. Lock only the measured real-time working set; memory locking bounds one delay source, not every source of lateness.

cards.front: What do POSIX.4 signals and sigqueue add?
cards.back: Real-time signals can be queued and prioritised rather than silently coalesced. sigqueue(pid, sig, value) sends a signal with application data in sigval ; explain delivery and handler safety within the stated process model.

cards.front: What does minimum Hamming distance tell you?
cards.back: Hamming distance is the number of differing bit positions. A code with minimum distance d min detects up to d min − 1 errors and corrects up to ⌊( d min − 1) / 2⌋ errors.

cards.front: Compare Hamming (7, 4) with 8-bit ASCII plus one parity bit.
cards.back: Hamming (7, 4) has d min = 3: it corrects one-bit errors and detects two-bit errors. A single parity bit gives d min = 2: it detects any odd number of bit errors but corrects none and misses even-numbered errors.

cards.front: RAID-0 versus RAID-1 versus RAID-5?
cards.back: RAID-0 stripes for performance with no redundancy. RAID-1 mirrors data, trading capacity for resilience and read performance. RAID-5 stripes data with distributed parity, tolerates one disk failure, and has parity-write overhead.

cards.front: How does backward recovery support dynamic software redundancy?
cards.back: Save a consistent checkpoint; on detected error or exception, restore it and retry with an alternative computation or replica. Record, compensate, or make external side effects idempotent—rollback cannot unsend an effect.

cards.front: What are FMV, GMV, FPV, and weighted averaging?
cards.back: They are voter rules for redundant outputs: formalised majority voter, generalised median voter, formalised plurality voter, and weighted averaging. State the rule first, then apply it to the supplied outputs.

cards.front: How do Lamport clocks work, and what do they miss?
cards.back: Increment the local counter before each local or send event; attach it to messages; on receipt set L = max( L , L msg ) + 1. If a happened-before b , then L ( a ) < L ( b ); the reverse does not prove causality or rule out concurrency.

cards.front: How do vector clocks capture causality?
cards.back: Keep one counter per process; increment the local entry before local or send events; on receipt take the component-wise maximum, then increment the receiver’s entry. V a < V b means happened-before; incomparable vectors mean concurrent events.

cards.front: Why was HTTP/2 developed, and what are its key features?
cards.back: It addresses HTTP/1 inefficiencies such as many connections and poor request use. Key features include binary framing, stream multiplexing, header compression, and prioritisation; its streams still run over TCP.

cards.front: What is TCP transport-level head-of-line blocking?
cards.back: TCP delivers one ordered byte stream. A lost earlier segment prevents delivery of later bytes, even when those bytes belong to an unrelated HTTP/2 application stream.

cards.front: How does QUIC avoid transport-level head-of-line blocking?
cards.back: QUIC has independently ordered streams, so loss in one stream need not delay delivery in another. Congestion control and a shared path can still slow the whole connection.

cards.front: How does QUIC connection establishment differ from TCP plus TLS?
cards.back: QUIC runs over UDP and integrates TLS into its transport handshake, allowing fewer setup round trips in favourable cases. It does not remove RTT, packet loss, or server-processing delay.

cards.front: What does congestion control do in QUIC?
cards.back: It infers congestion from signals such as loss and RTT, adjusts sending behaviour, and seeks to avoid persistent queues while balancing throughput and latency. In an answer, connect the action to the observed symptom.

cards.front: Throughput fairness versus latency fairness?
cards.back: Throughput fairness shares capacity comparably. Latency fairness prevents one flow imposing excessive queueing delay on another. The trade-off is harder to reason about when TCP and QUIC share a bottleneck.

cards.front: Why encrypt QUIC transport metadata?
cards.back: Encryption protects users and reduces unwanted middlebox ossification. The trade-off is less passive network visibility, so operators need endpoint telemetry such as qLog or authorised inspection.

cards.front: What do Wireshark, qLog, and qViz each contribute?
cards.back: Wireshark shows packet-level traffic but encrypted QUIC limits interpretation. qLog records endpoint transport events; qViz visualises those timelines to diagnose streams, loss, and congestion.

cards.front: What can a resource waterfall reveal?
cards.back: It separates connection, request waiting or first byte, and transfer stages. Use it to distinguish server or queueing delay from slow download, then corroborate the diagnosis with other evidence.

cards.front: What is QUIC connection migration?
cards.back: After path validation, a connection can continue when a client changes networks, for example Wi-Fi → 5G. It reduces disruption from address changes but does not guarantee that no freeze occurs.

cards.front: How does QUIC loss recovery help a real-time application?
cards.back: Packet numbers, acknowledgements, and timers identify loss; required stream data is retransmitted in a new packet. Independent streams avoid transport head-of-line blocking, while congestion control limits sending under loss.

cards.group: Soft Real-Time, QoS And Cloud Gaming
cards.front: Why is latency critical in a soft real-time system?
cards.back: Late output can still be correct but less useful: it can cause missed interaction, stutter, or degraded control quality. Trace where latency enters the system and explain the user-visible effect rather than treating it as an abstract number.

cards.group: Soft Real-Time, QoS And Cloud Gaming
cards.front: Intrinsic QoS versus perceived QoS or QoE?
cards.back: Intrinsic QoS is measured delivery quality such as delay, jitter, loss, and bitrate. Perceived QoS or QoE is the user’s experienced responsiveness, smoothness, and quality. Good metrics help explain, but do not automatically guarantee, good experience.

cards.group: Soft Real-Time, QoS And Cloud Gaming
cards.front: What does a jitter buffer do, and how do fixed and adaptive strategies differ?
cards.back: It delays playout to smooth packet-delay variation. A fixed buffer is simple but cannot adapt; an adaptive buffer changes depth as conditions change. Larger buffers reduce underflows but add interaction latency.

cards.group: Soft Real-Time, QoS And Cloud Gaming
cards.front: What is the end-to-end response-delay budget in cloud gaming?
cards.back: Trace user input, game processing, encoding, queueing, network transmission, loss recovery, decoding, buffering, and playout to the visible response. More bandwidth alone may not fix lag if processing, RTT, jitter, loss, or buffering dominates.

cards.group: Soft Real-Time, QoS And Cloud Gaming
cards.front: How does adaptive-bitrate streaming work, and why is it insufficient by itself for interactive use?
cards.back: The client estimates available conditions and selects segment representations to balance continuity, quality, rebuffering risk, and latency. It cannot remove input, processing, RTT, or playout delay, so it is only one control in an interactive system.

cards.group: Soft Real-Time, QoS And Cloud Gaming
cards.front: What do LCP, FID, and CLS measure?
cards.back: LCP measures perceived loading of the largest content; FID measures input responsiveness delay; CLS measures unexpected visual movement during loading.

cards.group: Soft Real-Time, QoS And Cloud Gaming
cards.front: How is Cumulative Layout Shift calculated?
cards.back: For each unexpected shift, CLS contribution = impact fraction × distance fraction; sum the contributions. The impact fraction is the viewport fraction covered by unstable before-and-after areas, and the distance fraction is the largest movement relative to the viewport.

sheets.title: Concurrency and Priority Protocols
sheets.purpose: Shared resources make a high-priority real-time task wait. Priority protocols make that wait bounded and reduce the risk that unrelated medium-priority work extends it.
refresher: Priority inversion H waits on L while M preempts L.

practice.title: Practice question 1 [medium/hard]
practice.prompt: L holds mutex M; H then blocks on M; medium-priority task X becomes ready. Draw the priority-inversion outcome and apply priority inheritance. [8 marks]
practice.route: Without inheritance, X pre-empts L, so H waits indirectly for arbitrary X work. With inheritance, L temporarily executes at H’s priority until it releases M; H then runs and L returns to its base priority. This bounds the inversion to L’s critical section (subject to nested locks/analysis), not to all low-priority computation.
practice.answer: Without inheritance, X pre-empts L, so H waits indirectly for arbitrary X work. With inheritance, L temporarily executes at H’s priority until it releases M; H then runs and L returns to its base priority. This bounds the inversion to L’s critical section (subject to nested locks/analysis), not to all low-priority computation.

practice.title: Practice question 2 [medium/hard]
practice.prompt: Two tasks acquire S1/S2 in opposite orders. Explain why priority inheritance is insufficient and how priority ceiling prevents the unsafe acquisition. [9 marks]
practice.route: Inheritance addresses unbounded blocking after contention; it does not break a circular wait where each task holds one lock. Under a ceiling protocol, each resource has the priority of its highest possible user and a task may acquire a resource only when its priority is above the current system ceiling (apart from its own locks). This blocks the second unsafe acquisition before a deadlock arises.

practice.title: Practice-source note
practice.prompt: The added questions synthesise recurring local CT420 paper patterns: scheduling calculations, time synchronisation, priority protocols, QUIC analysis, QoS and fault tolerance. They are not presented as exact wording from a named year.

mistakes: Calling any waiting deadlock; deadlock needs a circular wait/no progress argument.
Saying inheritance makes the low task permanently high priority.
Ignoring critical-section length in a timing claim.

sheets.title: Fault Tolerance and Redundancy
sheets.purpose: Fault tolerance keeps a service safe or available despite faults. A strong answer distinguishes detecting an error, masking it, recovering, and preventing a common-mode failure.

practice.title: Practice question 1 [medium/hard]
practice.prompt: Design a probe controller using RAID-5 storage, SEC RAM and hardware redundancy. Explain which fault/error/failure each layer addresses. [9 marks]
practice.route: A hardware fault (e.g. disk bit failure) can cause a corrupted stored value (error) and then a missed control action (failure). RAID-5 stripes data with distributed parity so one failed disk is reconstructed; SEC memory corrects a single-bit error (and should signal uncorrectable patterns); independent duplicated controllers with a voter can mask one controller output fault. Independence matters: identical power, software or environmental faults can defeat all replicas.

practice.title: Practice question 2 [medium/hard]
practice.prompt: A service can either checkpoint/rollback or run N-version implementations with voting. Choose for a non-idempotent booking transaction and justify. [8 marks]
practice.route: Checkpoint/rollback restores a prior consistent state but must coordinate external effects: once a booking email/payment leaves the system, replay may duplicate it unless it is logged/idempotent. N-version voting can mask some design faults but costs diverse implementations and a correct voter; common-specification faults remain. For the transaction, durable idempotency/logging plus checkpointed recovery is usually primary; use voting only where independent implementations and a well-defined output justify it.

sheets.title: Protocol Analysis Tools
sheets.purpose: Wireshark, qlog and qvis/qViz help diagnose protocol timing and behaviour. In exams, state what you would measure, how you would filter/visualise it, and the conclusion it can support.

practice.title: Practice question 1 [medium/hard]
practice.prompt: A QUIC video stream stalls while other streams continue. Specify an evidence plan using packet capture, qlog and qvis. [9 marks]
practice.route: Wireshark can show UDP/QUIC packet timing and transport symptoms but encryption limits application/stream interpretation without keys. Collect endpoint qlog events for stream state, packet loss, congestion window and recovery; load them into qvis to correlate timelines and identify whether the stalled stream is flow-control, server scheduling or loss recovery. Align host clocks and preserve trace IDs.

sheets.title: QUIC, HTTP/2 and HTTP/3
sheets.purpose: Recent material asks why modern web transports improve setup, multiplexing and recovery. Avoid feature lists: make a cause-and-effect comparison.

practice.title: Practice question 1 [medium/hard]
practice.prompt: Compare first-request setup for TCP+TLS and QUIC for a latency-sensitive game client; include the 0-RTT caveat. [9 marks]
practice.route: TCP requires transport setup then TLS negotiation before application data; QUIC integrates TLS over UDP and can reduce round trips, while a resumed connection may send 0-RTT data. 0-RTT data can be replayed, so use it only for idempotent/safe requests, not “buy item.” QUIC’s benefit is reduced establishment delay, not immunity from network latency or server processing.

practice.title: Practice question 2 [medium/hard]
practice.prompt: One lost TCP segment delays unrelated HTTP/2 streams; explain why HTTP/3 over QUIC changes the outcome and what congestion control still does. [8 marks]
practice.route: HTTP/2 multiplexes logical streams but TCP delivers one ordered byte stream, so a loss can cause transport head-of-line blocking for later bytes of other streams. QUIC gives streams independent ordering, so loss in one stream need not stall delivery in another. The shared connection still performs congestion control and reduces sending when it infers congestion, protecting the network but potentially increasing latency.

sheets.title: Real-time Foundations
sheets.purpose: Real-time engineering makes a result useful at the required time . The central exam habit is to name the timing requirement, the consequence of missing it, and the metric that exposes the problem.

practice.title: Practice question 1 [medium/hard]
practice.prompt: A controller has 8 ms computation, 4 ms queueing and 6 ms network delay against a 15 ms hard deadline. Assess it and give targeted improvements. [8 marks]
practice.route: End-to-end delay is 8+4+6=18 ms, so it misses by 3 ms; for a hard system this is failure, not merely low throughput. Profile the dominant stages, bound queueing with admission/priority control, reduce WCET or network delay, and remeasure worst-case rather than mean. A faster average CPU does not prove a deadline.

practice.title: Practice question 2 [medium/hard]
practice.prompt: For tasks (C,T)=(1,4),(1,5),(2,10) with D=T, use EDF and state the proof assumptions. [8 marks]
practice.route: U=1/4+1/5+2/10=0.25+0.20+0.20=0.65≤1. On one ideal pre-emptive processor with independent periodic tasks, negligible overhead and D=T, EDF is feasible by the utilisation condition. If blocking, release jitter, non-pre-emption or D<T is introduced, the conclusion needs a fuller analysis.

sheets.title: Scheduling and Schedulability
sheets.purpose: Scheduling decides which ready task runs. In an exam, calculate the stated test carefully, then explain what its pass or failure does (and does not) prove.

practice.title: Practice question 1 [medium/hard]
practice.prompt: Under pre-emptive RM with no blocking, analyse τ1=(1,4), τ2=(2,5), τ3=(4,20), all D=T. The RM bound fails; decide τ3 by response-time analysis. [9 marks]
practice.route: Priorities are τ1,τ2,τ3. U=.25+.4+.2=.85, above the three-task sufficient bound ≈.779, so failure is inconclusive. Iterate R3=4+ceil(R3/4)·1+ceil(R3/5)·2: 4→7→10→11→13→14→14. Thus R3=14≤20; R1=1≤4 and R2=3≤5, so all meet deadlines under the model.

practice.title: Practice question 2 [medium/hard]
practice.prompt: Construct an EDF-feasible but non-RM-feasible task set, then explain the evidence required. [8 marks]
practice.route: Use a known constrained-deadline/task example only after listing C,T,D and releases; compute total utilisation, draw the relevant timeline and perform RM response-time/schedulability analysis. Credit comes from a concrete counterexample, not the assertion that EDF is “better.” Under D=T on one processor, EDF U≤1 is its classic condition; RM needs its own analysis.

sheets.title: Soft Real-time and Multimedia
sheets.purpose: Multimedia often tolerates an occasional miss but users notice stalls, late audio and unstable interaction. A good answer connects network behaviour to user experience and the mitigation's cost.

practice.title: Practice question 1 [medium/hard]
practice.prompt: A VoIP path varies from 30–70 ms network delay. Compare a fixed 40 ms jitter buffer with an adaptive buffer. [8 marks]
practice.route: A fixed 40 ms buffer can smooth the observed variation if correctly sized, giving steady playout but adding interaction delay even when the network is good. An adaptive buffer changes target delay as jitter changes, reducing underflows or unnecessary latency but needs stable estimation and bounded adjustment. Packet loss may need concealment/FEC, not ever more buffering.

practice.title: Practice question 2 [medium/hard]
practice.prompt: Cloud gaming has high average bandwidth but feels slow and jerky. Diagnose QoS versus QoE and choose controls. [9 marks]
practice.route: Decompose input, encode, queue, network, decode and playout delay; variable queueing causes jitter and high end-to-end latency, while loss causes visible gaps. These are intrinsic QoS measures; the player’s responsiveness/quality judgement is QoE. Use queue management/priority, adaptive bitrate/FEC or concealment, and reduce avoidable encode/playout buffering, acknowledging the smoothness-versus-latency trade-off.

sheets.title: Time Synchronisation
sheets.purpose: Distributed devices need a shared notion of time for ordering, control and measurement. NTP targets robust network synchronisation; PTP targets high accuracy on suitable networks.
refresher: Offset difference, skew rate, accuracy reference, stability consistency.

practice.title: Practice question 1 [medium/hard]
practice.prompt: NTP timestamps are t1=100, t2=112, t3=120, t4=134 ms. Compute round-trip delay and offset using server-minus-client convention. [8 marks]
practice.route: RTD=(t4−t1)−(t3−t2)=(34)−(8)=26 ms. Offset=((t2−t1)+(t3−t4))/2=(12−14)/2=−1 ms, so the server is 1 ms behind the client under this convention. The 12/14 ms directional components reveal asymmetry, which biases the offset estimate.

practice.title: Practice question 2 [medium/hard]
practice.prompt: Choose NTP or PTP for a factory with most hosts needing milliseconds and a robot cell needing 100 µs. Explain clock mechanisms. [9 marks]
practice.route: Use robust NTP for ordinary hosts where millisecond accuracy is sufficient. For the cell use PTP with a selected grandmaster, hardware timestamping close to the NIC, and boundary/transparent clocks as suited to the topology; transparent clocks correct switch residence time, while P2P/E2E delay mechanisms estimate link delay. Monitor offset and provide redundancy; neither protocol promises perfect time.
